title: Dangote Says Lamu Refinery Could Generate 1,000MW of Power
desc: Aliko Dangote says the planned Lamu refinery could generate 1,000MW, with 500MW potentially supplied to Kenya’s government.
content:
Aliko Dangote has said the planned Dangote East Africa Refinery in Lamu will include a power-generation facility capable of producing about 1,000 megawatts (MW), with half of that capacity potentially supplied to the Kenyan government.

Dangote made the remarks in Lagos on Friday, September 25, while hosting President William Ruto during the President’s visit to Dangote’s refinery in Lekki, Nigeria. The development was reported in Kenya on Saturday, September 26.

According to Dangote, the Lamu project is expected to produce about 1,000MW of electricity, of which 500MW could be sold to the Kenyan government. He presented the power-generation component as part of the wider investment planned for Lamu.

The announcement comes days before the planned groundbreaking of the refinery project in Lamu, scheduled for September 30. A separate development on Saturday saw a vessel carrying 2,930 metric tonnes of heavy machinery arrive at the Port of Lamu ahead of the planned groundbreaking.

The refinery itself is planned with a processing capacity of up to 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day. The project is expected to form part of a larger industrial development around Lamu rather than operate solely as a petroleum-processing facility.

President Ruto has meanwhile said the Kenyan government is fully behind the project and that the land required for the development has been secured. He also said the government was working to remove administrative and bureaucratic obstacles that could delay implementation.

For Kenya, the proposed 500MW supply is potentially significant because it would add another planned source of electricity to the country's power system. However, the 1,000MW generation figure and proposed 500MW sale are Dangote's stated plans, not electricity already available to consumers.

The September 30 groundbreaking will therefore mark an important next stage for the project, while construction and the eventual power-generation arrangements will determine when the proposed capacity can actually be delivered.
